property_summary: For any deployed product contract, maintenance() must return the stored maintenance parameter (the value set at initialize); the mutant that returns constant ONE violates this because there exist initialized maintenance values not equal to ONE.

For any stored maintenance parameter value x set via initialize, calling maintenance(account) returns that stored UFixed18 x (the reference returns the stored value for every input); the mutant that unconditionally returns ONE violates this whenever the initialized maintenance != ONE (the fuzzer will find such inputs).

For any initialized maintenance parameter value m (set via ProductInfo.maintenance), calling maintenance(account) returns that stored UFixed18 m; the mutant that always returns UFixed18Lib.ONE will differ whenever the initialized maintenance != ONE (the fuzzer will find such m).

For every initialized product, calling maintenance(account) returns the stored maintenance parameter; the mutant that always returns UFixed18Lib.ONE violates this whenever the initialized maintenance differs from ONE (which the fuzzer can find).

For any initialization maintenance value m, the deployed reference contract returns that stored maintenance m via maintenance(account) for every account; the mutant that hardcodes maintenance() = ONE will differ whenever m != ONE (the fuzzer can find such m).

Calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) always updates the stored maintenance() to equal newMaintenance in the reference contract; the mutant emits the event but does not change the stored maintenance value, causing a mismatch for some inputs.

For every caller who is the product owner and any newMaintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) updates the contract's stored maintenance() to equal the provided newMaintenance (the reference preserves state), whereas the mutant only emits an event and does not change stored maintenance (so maintenance() remains the old value).

For any newMaintenance value and any caller who is the product owner, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) causes the contract's stored maintenance() to equal newMaintenance (reference); the mutant only emits the event and does not update stored maintenance(), breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller that is the product owner and any newMaintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) will leave maintenance() equal to newMaintenance afterwards in the correct contract, whereas the mutant emits the event but does not change stored maintenance(), so maintenance() can remain the previous value (the test fuzzes owner identity and newMaintenance to find a case distinguishing them).

For any caller that is the product owner and any newMaintenance value, after calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) the contract's maintenance() equals the provided newMaintenance in the correct contract; the mutant emits the event but does not update stored maintenance(), so maintenance() can remain unchanged and thus differ for some inputs.

Calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) emits exactly one MaintenanceUpdated event and sets maintenance() to newMaintenance; the mutant double-stores/emits it twice (so event count/order differs) and may produce two events whereas reference produces one for any input.

Calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) on the correct contract always results in maintenance() equaling newMaintenance (single successful update), whereas the mutant that calls the internal updater twice can be distinguished because the second internal call may trigger interactions (via settleProduct) that make the external call revert for some inputs — so the property: for all newMaintenance values, updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) does not revert and leaves maintenance() == newMaintenance; the mutant can cause a revert for some inputs.

For any arbitrary UFixed18 value passed to updateMaintenance, the correct contract accepts the call (does not revert) and afterwards maintenance() equals the passed value; the mutant that calls the internal updater twice can cause the external call to revert for some inputs (due to the extra settleProduct interaction), so the property will fail for that mutant for some fuzz inputs.

For any UFixed18 maintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) succeeds (does not revert) on the correct contract and leaves maintenance() equal to newMaintenance; the mutant that double-calls the internal updater can cause the external call to revert for some inputs, violating this property.

For every UFixed18 value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) on the correct contract completes without reverting and afterwards maintenance() equals newMaintenance; the mutant that double-stores may cause the external call to revert for some inputs (due to the extra settleProduct interaction), thus violating the property for some fuzzed inputs.

For any newMaintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) results in maintenance() returning that same newMaintenance (reference), whereas the mutant stores ZERO instead and thus maintenance() == 0 for some non-zero inputs.

For any UFixed18 newMaintenance value passed to updateMaintenance, the correct contract stores that exact value so maintenance() == newMaintenance after the call; the mutant instead stores ZERO regardless, so for some non-zero newMaintenance the equality fails.

For any nonzero UFixed18 value x passed to updateMaintenance, the correct contract stores that value so maintenance() == x after the call; the mutant instead stores ZERO, so for some nonzero x the equality breaks.

For every UFixed18 value passed to updateMaintenance, the correct contract stores that exact value so maintenance() equals the passed value after the call; the mutant instead stores ZERO regardless, so there exist inputs (non-zero values) where maintenance() != newMaintenance.

For every arbitrary non-zero uint256 rawAmount interpreted as UFixed18.from(uint256), calling updateMaintenance with that value causes maintenance() to be non-zero afterwards in the correct contract, while the mutant sets maintenance() to zero for some non-zero inputs; equivalently: there exists some fuzzed uint256 input where maintenance() != 0 after the call on the reference (it must equal the provided non-zero value) but the mutant returns 0 — the test fuzzes a uint256 and asserts maintenance() != 0 after updateMaintenance when input encodes a non-zero UFixed18.

For any new maintenance value and caller owner, calling updateMaintenance on the correct contract always advances product state by calling settle (so latestVersion returned by latestVersion() after updateMaintenance equals the oracle latest version at time of settle), whereas the mutant that returns early before calling settle can leave latestVersion unchanged — the test fuzzes an owner address and a maintenance value and asserts that after updateMaintenance the contract's latestVersion is nonzero (i.e. settle ran and advanced state) which holds for the reference but can be false for the mutant.

For any owner caller and maintenance value, calling updateMaintenance on the correct contract always triggers an internal settle that advances latestVersion (latestVersion() > 0) while the mutant that returns early can leave latestVersion unchanged (== 0) for some inputs (owner & maintenance), so latestVersion() > 0 after updateMaintenance is a property the reference satisfies but the mutant can violate.

For any caller who is the product owner and any maintenance value, calling updateMaintenance must successfully complete and the contract's maintenance() getter must equal the provided value (reference: settle is called before storing new maintenance; mutant: skipping settle can leave behavior different or revert in some scenarios), so assert that maintenance() == newMaintenance after updateMaintenance — reference always holds, mutant can fail for some fuzzed owner/newMaintenance combos.

For any caller who is the product owner and any new maintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(...) on the correct contract must perform the settle side-effect before storing the new maintenance (so settle is invoked and returns the current oracle version), whereas the mutant that returns early from the settleProduct modifier can skip that settle; we detect this by ensuring that updateMaintenance emits the ClosedUpdated/Settle-related state change via calling updateMaintenance through a helper Product-like controller where settle would have advanced latestVersion — concretely we assert that after an owner calls updateMaintenance the contract's maintenance() equals the supplied value (reference always sets the maintenance and triggers settle), which the mutant can violate for some fuzzed owner/newMaintenance inputs.

For any caller who is the product owner and any new maintenance value, calling updateMaintenance(newMaintenance) completes successfully and stores the new maintenance value (maintenance() == newMaintenance); the mutant that returns early from the settleProduct modifier can skip necessary state progression and cause updateMaintenance to not persist the new maintenance for some owner/maintenance inputs.

For any caller who is the product owner, calling updateFundingFee(newFee) on the correct contract always performs a settle (so the external call to controller.collateral().settleProduct is invoked as part of settle path and thus any settling side-effects occur) — the mutant that removed settleProduct allows updateFundingFee to complete without performing settle, so a side-effect observable through settle (here: the call to collateral.settleProduct which may revert when unsettled state triggers) can differ; the test fuzzes a boolean that controls whether collateral.settleProduct would revert, proving the mutant can bypass the settle and avoid the revert while the reference always triggers it.

For any caller who is the product owner and any funding fee value, calling updateFundingFee(newFee) on the correct contract always runs settle (so if settle causes collateral.settleProduct to revert due to a malicious collateral, updateFundingFee will revert); the mutant that removes the settle can return successfully even when settle would have reverted, so there exist inputs (a malicious collateral that reverts) where the mutant succeeds but the reference reverts.
